title: Zoom in: a price change removes every stale copy
caption: The change event comes from the DB's own log, so an update that commits is always followed by its invalidations.

messages.label: UPDATE products
messages.note: The DB is the source of truth; nothing is written to a cache here.

messages.label: row 42 changed
messages.note: A CDC connector tails the DB log, so even a writer that crashes right after commit can't skip the event.

messages.label: DEL product:42
messages.note: Delete, don't SET: the next reader loads the committed row.

messages.label: evict 42
messages.note: Pub/sub to every pod; the 5 s local TTL covers a pod that misses it.

messages.label: commit offset
messages.note: Only after the removals succeed, so a crash replays the event instead of losing it.

scenarios.name: Lost DEL
scenarios.summary: The DEL never arrives. Because the offset is committed only after success, the event is replayed and the key is removed late, not never.

messages.label: DEL product:42
messages.note: A network blip: the cache never sees the DEL and still holds price 89.

messages.label: GET product:42
messages.note: Readers see the old price until the retry.

messages.label: retry DEL product:42
messages.note: Offset not committed, so the invalidator retries with backoff.

scenarios.name: Alternative: TTL only
scenarios.summary: No invalidation pipeline at all: every copy lives for its TTL. Much simpler, and fine for descriptions and reviews, but a price can be wrong for the whole TTL.

messages.label: GET product:42
messages.note: Nobody told the cache: it still serves 89.

messages.label: TTL expires
messages.note: Staleness is bounded by the TTL, here up to 10 min.
